extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychoanalysis, aesthetics, and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Freud's theoretical criteria for different forms of the comic (wit, naive, motion, situation, expectation, caricature, unmasking, etc.) as psychological mechanisms that produce comic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naive (naive-comic) as a form of the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: The naive would thus be a form of the comic, in so far as its pleasure originates from the difference in expenditure which results in our effort to understand the other person; and it resembles wit through the condition that the expenditure saved by the comparison must be an inhibition expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'naive joke' and 'naive obscenity'. The pleasure added by naive speeches is labelled 'comical' pleasure; the mechanism is an economy in inhibition that arises from comparing another's utterance or behavior with our own. Study naive via these examples rather than assuming identical mechanisms to wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic pleasure arises from economized expenditure via comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic pleasure originates through an economized expenditure by comparing the utterance or action of someone else with our own; a difference in expenditure that becomes capable of discharge yields pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the general theoretical principle underlying many comic forms: comparison produces a surplus (or deficit) of expenditure (often inhibition expenditure) which, if unused, can be discharged as comic pleasure. Freud contrasts this with explanations based on attention-fluctuation and rejects those.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of attention-fluctuation explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure does not originate through the fluctuation of our attention to and fro between contrasting ideas; instead, the comparing of contrasts results in a difference in expenditure which, if not used, becomes capable of discharge and hence a source of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud explicitly disputes authors who locate comic pleasure in shifting attention; use expenditure-comparison rather than attention-fluctuation when explaining comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occurrence as unintentional discovery in social relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The comical appears primarily as an unintentional discovery in the social relations of human beings; it is found in persons — in their movements, shapes, actions, and characteristic traits — and later in their mental qualities and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can also be found in animals and inanimate objects by personification. Recognize that comic elements may be situational and not intrinsic to the person alone; one can induce comic situations deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of motion (immoderate/inappropriate expenditure)
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh at immoderate and inappropriate actions because they appear to us as an excessive expenditure of energy; we compare the motions observed in others with those we ourselves would produce, using our own innervation-expenditure as the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: clown pantomime, exaggerated movements, child's extra motions while learning to write, bowler's follow-through. Mechanism: perception evokes ideational imitation and comparison of mobilized innervation; when the other's motion shows superfluous expenditure relative to our standard, it becomes comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideational mimicry / innervation representation of magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of motions are accompanied by innervations to muscles that represent a quantitative factor; the conception of greater motions is accompanied by greater ideational innervation, i.e., 'ideational mimicry' represents bigness/smallness in ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: speakers use gestures/voice/face to depict size/intensity (big mountain vs little dwarf). This ideational mimicry underlies expectation and perception mechanics that produce comic effects when mismatches occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception evokes imitative impulse leading to comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceiving another's motion produces an impulse to conceive or imitate it; by imaginatively performing the motion we compare the required expenditures and detect where one expended more energy, producing comic surplus if the other's expenditure is superfluous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation need not be overt; memory traces and ideational substitutes suffice. The comparison relies on an internally represented innervation-expenditure for the motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of two kinds of expenditure as pleasure-sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter results from comparing different expenditures (identification/apperception expenditure vs normal expenditure) and finding a surplus or deficit that can be discharged; this comparative mechanism is central across comic types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud frames many comic species (motion, psychic attributes, situation, expectation) as instantiations of this comparison of expenditures (e.g., Einfühlungsaufwand vs usual expenditure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in psychic/mental attributes (nonsense/foolishness)
rubrics_metrics.description: In psychic activities it is comical if the other person economizes in expenditure which we consider indispensable; nonsense and foolishness are perceived as inferior (too little mental expenditure) and thus become comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the reverse of comic motion: there the other expends too much somatic energy; in psychic comic the other expends too little mental energy. Examples: ignorant students' comical nonsense. Cultural development (more mental, less somatic work) frames this preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling of superiority is related but not essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughing often expresses a pleasurably perceived superiority adjudged to ourselves in comparison, but Freud notes that the feeling of superiority bears no essential relations to comic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce all comic pleasure to mere feeling of superiority; comparative expenditure and discharge are the principal mechanism though superiority may accompany it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of situation (identification with altered expenditure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic of situation arises when pleasure-producing difference of energy expenditures comes into existence through outer influences (a 'situation') — we laugh when we admit that had we been placed in the same situation we should have done the same thing; the person becomes comical through inferiority relative to his former ego.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a person engrossed in an activity suddenly disturbed by pain or excremental need; the comic depends on identification and the recognition that one's former intensive interest is now diminished by disturbance. The comic of situation draws on conventions/necessities of society and bodily needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of expectation (preparatory motor expenditure and disappointment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation involves quantitatively determined preparatory expenditures (motor preliminaries, tension of senses); when expectation is disappointed the mobilized expenditure is superfluous and yields comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: preparing to catch a ball that turns out light; lifting a basket thought heavy but hollow; Pavlov's dogs' salivation varying with expectation. Consider components: conceptual mimicry (bigness/smallness), attention-tension (expectation expenditure), and abstraction expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature as isolation and exaggeration of a comical feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Caricature produces comedy by rendering prominent one feature (comic in itself) from the picture of the exalted object — isolating and exaggerating it so the comic effect spreads over the whole picture; when a comical feature is lacking caricature can create one by exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition: presence of the exalted must not force reverence. Caricature may falsify reality yet still produce comic pleasure; it's a technique of degradation by exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as a comic-making device
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation accords the hearer an extraordinary amount of pleasure and makes its subject comic even without the exaggeration of caricature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation can be used playfully or aggressively; it's a milder means than caricature but still a deliberate production of comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making oneself comical vs authentic comicality (shamming)
rubrics_metrics.description: One may purposely make oneself appear awkward or stupid and thus produce the comic 'exactly as if one were really so'; but if the audience knows the actor is only shamming, the feeling of superiority in the audience does not arise — this shows the comic is independent of feeling-of-superiority in principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under some circumstances, purposeful comic performance can even secure admiration. Distinguish audience awareness of sham when analyzing comic reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody, travesty, unmasking: destroying uniformity to degrade the exalted
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody and travesty destroy uniformity between known attributes of illustrious persons and their speech/actions by replacing either; unmasking reveals that someone who commands dignity is merely human, exposing psychic automatism and thereby producing comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: witticisms that unmask marriage agents or a fashionable lady whose cry reveals ordinary pain; these may serve as facades for wit but function structurally as comic unmasking. Use to undermine authority or dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques of making a person comical (transfer, disguise, imitations, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods to make someone comical include transfer into comic situations, imitations, disguise, unmasking, caricature, parody, travesty, and similar means; these can be real (practical jokes) or feigned (speech/play).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These techniques may be used for amusement or as instruments of aggression to render a person contemptible or deprive dignity. Practical examples: tripping someone, exploiting credulity, placing someone in a comic situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic used as instrument of aggression or degradation
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques for making a person comical may serve hostile or aggressive tendencies — to render him contemptible or deprive him of claims to dignity and authority — though spontaneous comic need not have such motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize ethical/social dimension: comic-making can degrade and humiliate; the same mechanisms that produce harmless amusement can be directed to mock or attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection of wit and comic via unmasking and unconscious processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and the comic can unite when wit-work reopens hidden sources of comic pleasure (e.g., unmasking psychic automatism) or when wit supplies compromises via unconscious/faulty-thinking modes; some comic stories double as wit when they mask deeper opposite expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: marriage-agent anecdotes that both unmask and, for perceptive readers, function as wit. When analyzing a joke, consider both surface comic-unmasking and deeper wit-work (compromise with rational critic).
